name: Text to Video, Physics and Continuity
title: Text to Video, Physics and Continuity
answer: Text to video with physics and continuity concerns generation of moving image sequences from natural language prompts where objects obey basic physical rules and scenes remain consistent across frames. This includes gravity, collision, fluid motion, lighting persistence, character identity, and camera movement. The page sits within cinematography and video synthesis, focusing on how generated shots hold up as continuous footage rather than as isolated stills. It covers both short clips and longer sequences where a prompt describes an action or event.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These models run on large GPU clusters, typically using diffusion transformers or autoregressive video predictors trained on paired text and video data. Training requires substantial video corpora, often scraped from the web, and inference is compute heavy, with a single short clip taking seconds to minutes on professional hardware. Many commercial systems are accessed through cloud APIs, while open weight models can run locally on high end workstations. The site tracks 1000 video models, though only a subset address physical plausibility directly.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by encoding a text prompt into a latent representation, then denoising or predicting video tokens in a sequence that is decoded into frames. Continuity is improved through temporal attention layers, optical flow priors, or physics simulators that guide the generation. Artists often iterate by adjusting prompts, using negative prompts to suppress impossible motion, or generating multiple seeds and selecting the most coherent take. Some pipelines combine a generated base video with post processing tools for stabilization or frame interpolation.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on training data provenance, because many video models are trained on copyrighted footage without clear licenses. Generated clips can reproduce distinctive actors, locations, or camera moves from the training set, raising likeness and copyright questions. Continuity failures can also create misleading footage, such as a person appearing to perform an action they never did, which matters for documentary or news contexts. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, though none are named here, and artists should check terms of service before commercial use.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward longer, physically stable sequences with persistent object identity and editable camera paths. Research is combining neural generation with lightweight physics engines so that collisions, fluids, and shadows behave correctly without full simulation. Expect better control over motion through keyframes, depth maps, and motion brushes, as well as lower cost inference that makes iterative direction practical. The next step is likely multi shot generation where a character and environment remain consistent across cuts.
